summary:
La Guajira stands under Colombia's national legal framework, which the national record sets out in full; the department's own documented signal is a campaign of written threats by armed groups. Since March 2024 armed groups operating in the department have circulated flyers carrying a kill list of named individuals, stating that "all will be military targets" and listing "homosexuals, lesbians, rapists, trans" among those designated. The wording places trans people in a category of persons marked for lethal violence, and it names individuals rather than issuing a general warning.

A trans visitor's exposure in La Guajira is therefore tied to where armed-group control is exercised rather than to the formal legal position, which is protective. The threat instrument is a written list distributed publicly, so visibility of a trans person to neighbours and to whoever posts the flyers is the operative risk factor in those areas.

Armed groups in Colombia's conflict-affected departments have used flyer campaigns of this kind to force trans women out of their homes and towns, and displacement rather than protection is the documented response available to those named. La Guajira has no separate legal regime of its own; the national protections apply here as elsewhere in the country.
tangentialFactors:
Flyer campaigns of this type are not confined to one department: armed groups in several of Colombia's conflict-affected departments have used written lists and messaging applications to declare trans people military targets, and the practice forms part of territorial control rather than a discrete local incident.

The La Guajira flyers' wording merges trans people with "rapists" in a single category of legitimate targets, a framing that classifies those named as criminals as well as security objectives.
localsOnly:
For trans people living in La Guajira, the flyers are the most concrete documented threat: they name individuals, they are distributed publicly, and they classify trans people among the categories the armed group claims a right to kill.

Displacement is the recourse documented for trans women targeted this way in Colombia's conflict-affected departments: leaving the town, sometimes more than once, rather than relying on police protection. Trans residents who are known in their community, or whose livelihood depends on visible public work, carry that exposure directly.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source reviewed establishes whether the La Guajira flyers remain in circulation, how many people are named on them, whether anyone listed has been killed or displaced, or whether the department's police or prosecutor's office has opened any investigation. Department-level figures for trans killings, for use of the notary procedure to change the sex marker, or for trans-specific health services in Riohacha or in Wayuu communities are likewise not sourced.

Reporting on armed-group targeting of trans people in Colombia is concentrated on other departments; the La Guajira picture rests on the flyer reports alone.
